Hey, sorry to bug you. I've been drafting a message to my ex for like two weeks and I need someone with fresh eyes to tell me if the tone works. We broke up back in June — it wasn't a big fight or anything, just wasn't working out — but there were some things I never got to say and I finally sat down and wrote them out.

Here's what I have:

---

Hey. First, this isn't meant to start a conversation. I've been sitting with things for a while and there are things I needed to say, and I didn't when we were together.

You were funny and I loved that about you, but the bit you'd do about how I just type emails all day — around Marc and Alex, over and over — that landed harder than I let on. I know it was a joke to you but it wasn't to me and you knew that and you still did it to try and get a laugh. It wasn't even funny.

And you knew what my mom's opinion about music school did to me, and you brought it up more than once when we were arguing when you knew how my mom treated me. It was like something you kept in your back pocket. That's the one I keep coming back to. That was a choice.

I don't think you did any of this to hurt me. I really don't. I think you did it because you could. I'm not looking for an apology, and honestly I don't want to talk about it. I just needed you to know I saw it clearly. I hope you're doing well.

---

Does that sound okay? I really don't want to come across as bitter or petty. I just want to say what I actually thought, calmly, and then move on. My friend read it and said I'm overthinking it, that I should just send it. But I keep almost sending it and then closing the app. Something keeps making me pause and I don't know what.

Does the tone read right?

Does the tone read right?

The tone reads right. It's not bitter and it's not petty — it's specific, which is actually the opposite of both. Bitter letters generalize ("you always," "you never"). Yours points at two things and says why they landed. That's the hardest version to dismiss, and it's the one that took you two weeks.

A few things I noticed as a reader:

"I don't think you did any of this to hurt me. I really don't. I think you did it because you could." That's the sharpest line in the letter, and I think it's the truest one. It's also the line most likely to be experienced as the harshest — not because it's unfair, but because it's accurate in a way that's hard to argue with. I'd keep it. I just want you to know it's doing more work than the sentences around it.

"It wasn't even funny" — that one reads differently from the rest. Everything else in the letter is you reporting your own experience, which is unarguable. That line is a verdict on their comedy, which is arguable, and it's the one place a defensive reader could grab hold and turn the whole thing into a debate about whether the bit was funny. It's also the most human line in there. Your call. But it's the crack in the door.

Two small things: "when you knew how my mom treated me" repeats "you knew" from earlier in the same sentence. And "I saw it clearly" is doing a lot at the end — it's good, it just might be stronger alone, without "I just needed you to know" in front of it.

On the pausing. I'd push back gently on your friend. "You're overthinking it, just send it" is advice for a different kind of message — the one where you're anxious about nothing. This isn't that. You wrote something that names a person's cruelty accurately and then closes the door on their reply. That's a real thing to do and it makes sense that your hand stops on the way to the button.

I'll say the part I actually think: the letter says "this isn't meant to start a conversation," and I believe you mean it. But you can't control whether they answer. If they write back with something defensive, or something sad, or nothing at all — any of those is a possible ending. The letter is finished. Whether you're finished is a separate question, and only you know that one.

It's a good letter. What happens if you don't send it?
